# When AI Sits Between a Job and a Person

## The Question

A job application may first go through software. A computer may screen a résumé, score a personality test, or judge a video. It may study a person's face, voice, and gestures. The applicant sees a job chance. The recruiter sees many applications. The owner sees a company decision. One screen creates three different experiences.

### Voice 1: The Applicant's Story

I speak to a camera. Software scores my voice, face, and gestures. I read about a woman who did well on a skills test. But AI gave her low scores for gestures and facial expressions. She later had no job for a long time. I also know about an applicant who said AI scored his reliability and honesty. He had no way to refuse the score or question it. I want people to see my skills and character. I do not want them reduced to one score.

### Voice 2: The Recruiter's Story

I start with résumés and an AI tool. It sorts résumés, sets interviews, and matches people with jobs. It helps when applications arrive faster than my team can read them. But a score does not finish the work. I may write a simple summary of a fairness check. I may also answer candidates' questions. One company's public notice shows this duty is real. I also judge résumés written by AI. Are they a useful skill, or do they show too little effort? I run the tool. But I do not decide if the company adopts it.

### Voice 3: The Business Owner's Story

Each week, I check the hiring dashboard. I look at time, cost, and the people we still need. If hiring slows, the work does not wait. I have read reports of faster hiring and lower costs after AI. That is why I may keep using it. But news of a tool that rated women lower makes me check my choice again. If people question it, my name is attached. I protect the company's future. But I also carry the risk of being wrong.

## Why They See It Differently

All three want the right person in the right job. But they face different problems. The applicant may lose a fair chance. The recruiter must keep work moving and explain the system. The owner must keep the company running and answer for the choice. The applicant cannot choose the system. The recruiter runs it and may help decide if the company adopts it. The owner may make the final choice. Outside rules limit all three roles. In New York City, an employer needs a recent fairness check. It also needs a public summary and notice before using an automated hiring tool. The recruiter cannot use the tool in secret. The owner cannot depend on speed alone. The applicant still cannot control the score. One company stopped a tool after it rated women lower. These views do not give one simple answer.

## What This Question Really Means

This is not only a question about a machine. It may read a résumé or study a face. It is also about who decides what a fair chance means. Who must explain the system? Who faces the results when it fails? Hiring is not only a choice about tools. It is also about power, proof, and responsibility.

【R1(本Trial、Revision前)】
# When AI Sits Between a Job and a Person

## A Faster Door That May Be Harder to Open

In September 2026, AI is part of hiring at many companies. It can read applications, score tests, set interview times, and judge video interviews. Companies want to hire faster and spend less money. But the same system can create three different problems. An applicant may not know why the door closed. A recruiter must explain whether the process was fair. An owner must choose between speed and serious legal and business risks.

### Voice 1: The Applicant — “I Need a Fair Chance”

I want my work and experience to decide whether I get an interview. I do not want a hidden score to decide my future before a person hears from me.

When an AI system reads my application, I may not know which words it wants. In a video interview, it may study my voice, face, or speaking style. But I may not know if those signs truly show how well I can do the job.

This fear is not only an idea. One applicant in Massachusetts said that a hiring system gave him scores for qualities such as trust and honesty. He said he could not refuse the AI interview. He also could not challenge the result. He was not hired.

That leaves me with no clear path. If I am rejected, I need to know what happened. I need a way to ask for a human review. Without that, I may feel that I was judged by a rule I could not see and could not question.

I understand that companies receive many applications. I also understand that people make mistakes. But if AI controls my chance to enter the process, I need a fair way to understand and question its decision.

### Voice 2: The Recruiter — “I Must Be Able to Explain It”

I use AI because hiring work can become too large for a small team. It can sort applications, plan interviews, and help write job posts. This gives me more time to speak with candidates and managers.

But I cannot simply say, “The computer chose you” or “The computer rejected you.” Candidates want to know if the process is fair. Many already believe that AI screening can be biased.

So I need more than a tool. I need records of how it works. I need clear information about what the system measures. I also need regular bias checks. If the results are different for different groups of people, I must see that problem and act on it.

I must prepare simple information for candidates. I should be able to tell them where AI is used and what happens next. If a candidate raises a concern, I need a real answer, not a general promise that the system is fair.

This creates pressure in my daily work. AI may save time, but I remain responsible for the hiring process. If I cannot explain a score, I cannot confidently use it. If I cannot show that the process is fair, the tool becomes a risk instead of help.

### Voice 3: The Business Owner — “I Must Protect the Company”

I look at every hiring cost. Open jobs can slow down the business. A long hiring process can make good candidates leave. AI may cut the time needed to find people from weeks to only a few days. It may also reduce hiring costs.

Those gains matter to me. They can help the company serve customers and keep operating. If I do not control costs, I may not be able to protect the jobs of the people already here.

But speed is not the only cost. If an AI system treats people unfairly, the company may face a legal claim. We may have to pay damages. We may also lose the trust of candidates, workers, and customers. A damaged name can stay with the company for years.

I therefore need to know more than whether the tool is fast. I need to know what it does when it makes a mistake. I need clear records, human checks, and a plan for complaints. These controls may slow hiring and cost money. Yet using the system without them could cost much more.

My decision is not simply “use AI” or “do not use AI.” I must decide whether the savings are worth the risks for this company, this job, and these candidates.

## The Same Tool, Three Different Pressures

These three needs do not fit together easily. The applicant wants a clear reason and a chance to challenge the result. That review takes time. The recruiter wants enough control and evidence to explain the process. Audits and records take staff and money. The owner wants the hiring process to stay fast and affordable. Extra steps can reduce the savings that made AI attractive.

A system can also look efficient from the owner’s desk while feeling unfair to the applicant. A recruiter may have a fairness document but still be unable to explain one person’s rejection. A human review may help one applicant, but it may also make the process slower for thousands of others.

The difficult question is therefore not only whether AI can find candidates quickly. It is whether the company can use it while giving each rejected person a meaningful explanation and a real way to raise a concern. The owner must pay for that protection. The recruiter must carry it out. The applicant must live with the result.

## The Decision Behind the Screen

AI can make hiring faster, but it cannot remove responsibility from the people who use it. An applicant still needs a fair chance. A recruiter still needs to prove that the process is fair. An owner still needs to protect the company from legal and financial harm.

For now, every company using AI faces this choice in practical terms: save time today, or spend more time checking the system before harm grows. The answer will shape not only how quickly a person is hired, but also whether that person can understand why the door opened—or why it closed.


【R2(本Trial、Family X既存R1→R2 Revision適用後)】
# When AI Sits Between a Job and a Person

## The Score Appears Before the Interview

The screen lights up. An applicant has finished a video interview. A recruiter waits for a score. A business owner watches the hiring clock. In September 2026, this scene is common at many companies. AI can read applications, score tests, arrange interviews, and study video interviews. It promises speed and lower costs. But behind the same screen are three people with three different fears. One wants a fair chance. One must explain the machine. One must protect the whole company.

### Voice 1: The Applicant — “Did I Lose to a Number?”

I press “send” on my application. Then I wait.

Maybe a person will read it. Maybe a computer will read it first. I may not know which words the system wants. I may not know what it sees as a strong answer.

Then comes the video interview. I speak to a camera, not a person. The system may study my face, my voice, and the way I speak. It may give me a score for qualities such as trust and honesty.

But can a face show honesty? Can a voice show how well I will do a job? If the answer is no, I may lose my chance before anyone meets me.

I think about an applicant in Massachusetts. In 2021, he applied for a supply-chain job at CVS Health. He took a video interview that used HireVue technology and AI from Affectiva to study facial expressions and voice tone. He said he could not refuse the AI process. He also said he could not challenge the result. He was not hired.

He sued CVS. Later, CVS agreed to a temporary settlement in a class-action case.

That story stays with me. If an AI score rejects me, what can I do? Can I ask for a human review? Can I explain something the system missed? Can I even find out what the system decided?

I understand why companies use AI. There may be thousands of applications. But I am not a line on a screen. I am a person waiting outside the hiring door. I need to know why the door opened for someone else—and why it closed for me.

### Voice 2: The Recruiter — “Now I Have to Question the Question”

My morning begins with a crowded hiring list. Applications wait. Interview times must be arranged. Managers want names. Candidates want answers.

AI can help. It can sort applications, plan interviews, and help write job posts. In a 2026 survey, 91 percent of HR leaders said they were actively using AI somewhere in hiring. Resume screening was the most common use.

The tool gives me speed. It also gives me a new job inside my job: I must check the checker.

A candidate may ask, “Was I rejected because of my experience, my answers, or an AI score?” I cannot answer, “The computer said no.” That is not an explanation.

Many job seekers already believe AI screening can be biased. So I need more than a friendly message. I need documents that show where AI is used. I need to explain what it measures. I need regular bias checks. I need records that show whether the system treats different groups differently.

I also need a plan for mistakes. If an applicant says, “This score is wrong,” someone must listen. If a person can review the decision, I must know when and how that review happens.

This is the strange part. AI was supposed to make my work lighter. Instead, it adds a new question to every hiring decision: Can I defend this choice?

I still need to fill the job. I still need to move quickly. But if I cannot explain the process, the fast tool becomes a slow-moving problem.

### Voice 3: The Business Owner — “The Clock Is Counting, but So Is the Risk”

I look at an empty position and see a clock.

While the job is open, work may slow down. Customers may wait. A strong candidate may accept another offer. Hiring can take weeks, and weeks cost money.

AI promises a faster race. Hilton has reported that its average hiring time fell from about six weeks to five days after using AI. IBM has reported a reduction in hiring costs of about 30 percent.

Those numbers catch my attention. Five days sounds better than six weeks. Lower costs sound better than higher costs. If the company cannot control its hiring costs, it may not be able to protect its business.

Then another clock starts.

What if the system treats an applicant unfairly? The company may face a discrimination claim. We may face legal responsibility and damages. Our reputation may also suffer. A company can lose trust much faster than it can build trust.

That loss may reach customers, workers, and future applicants. A quick hire may look good this month. A public problem may stay with us for years.

So I ask questions that do not fit neatly on a sales slide. Can we check the system? Can we show how it made a decision? Can a person review a result? Can we answer a complaint without saying, “We do not know”?

These checks cost time and money. They may make the hiring process less fast. But using AI without them may create a much larger bill.

I want the speed. I also want the company to survive the mistake that speed might hide.

## The Countdown Has Three Different Winners

The applicant sees a locked door. The recruiter sees a black box with a question mark. The owner sees a clock and a possible bill.

All three are looking at the same AI system. But their best results are different.

The applicant wants a clear reason and a real chance to challenge the score. The recruiter needs time to check the process and explain it. The owner wants the job filled quickly and the cost kept low.

These goals do not simply join together. A human review may help an applicant, but reviews take time. A bias audit may help a recruiter, but audits cost money. A faster system may help the owner, but speed does not prove fairness.

A report can say that the system works well. It may still fail to explain one person’s rejection. A company can save money on hiring. It may still pay much more after a discrimination claim. A recruiter can believe the process is fair. The applicant may still feel trapped inside a decision they cannot see.

The real contest is not only between people and machines. It is between three kinds of pressure: the need for a chance, the need for an explanation, and the need to protect the business.

## When the Screen Goes Dark

AI can move an application through the hiring process in seconds. It cannot answer every person who waits on the other side of the screen.

The applicant still needs a fair chance. The recruiter still needs proof that the process is fair. The owner still needs to weigh speed against legal, financial, and reputational risk.

That is why the decision is not a simple race between “use AI” and “do not use AI.” The harder question comes after the score appears:

Who will explain it?

If the answer is nobody, the company may save time today. But the applicant may lose a future, the recruiter may lose control of the process, and the owner may discover that the fastest hiring decision was the most expensive one.
